plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.3.3
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a polar rectangle R, the fundamental building block for polar double integration. The region R is bounded by two circular arcs r = 1.5 and r = 2 (solid blue curves) and two rays theta = pi/6 and theta = pi/4 (dashed red lines), forming a curved quadrilateral shaded in light blue and labeled R. The figure introduces the polar rectangle as the analogue of the Cartesian rectangle for setting up double integrals in polar coordinates, showing how its curved sides arise from the constant-r and constant-theta boundary conditions.

interactionPlan.concept: A polar rectangle is the region formed by holding radius between two constants and angle between two constants, so its constant-r sides are circular arcs and its constant-theta sides are rays.
elements: origin point where the polar rays begin
black horizontal polar axis extending rightward from the origin
lower dashed red ray labeled theta = pi/6
upper dashed red ray labeled theta = pi/4
inner solid blue circular arc labeled r = 1.5
outer solid blue circular arc labeled r = 2
light blue shaded annular sector between the two arcs and two rays
region label R centered inside the shaded polar rectangle
optional straight-sided Cartesian rectangle overlay with the same delta-r by delta-theta dimensions
labels for current r1, r2, theta1, and theta2 values

interactions.label: Inner radius r1
interactions.teaches: The inner boundary of a polar rectangle is a circular arc because every point on it has the same radius from the origin

interactions.label: Outer radius r2
interactions.teaches: Changing the outer radius expands or contracts the region radially while preserving the same angular wedge

interactions.label: Lower angle theta1
interactions.teaches: A constant-theta boundary is a straight ray from the origin, so changing theta rotates one side of the polar rectangle

interactions.label: Upper angle theta2
interactions.teaches: The angular width of the polar rectangle is the sweep between two rays, not a horizontal distance

interactions.label: Show Cartesian rectangle analogue
interactions.teaches: A polar rectangle plays the role of a Cartesian rectangle in integration, but its constant-radius sides curve because radius is measured from the origin

demo_steps.title: Identify the four polar bounds
demo_steps.narration: The region R is trapped between r = 1.5 and r = 2, and between theta = pi/6 and theta = pi/4. Two boundaries are circular arcs and two are rays from the origin.

demo_steps.title: Change the radial bounds
demo_steps.narration: Move r1 or r2 to resize the region inward or outward. The angular rays stay fixed, while the blue circular arcs move because they represent constant radius.

demo_steps.title: Change the angular bounds
demo_steps.narration: Move theta1 or theta2 to rotate the red rays. The same radial band now covers a different angular sweep.

demo_steps.title: Compare with a Cartesian rectangle
demo_steps.narration: Turn on the straight-sided overlay to see the analogy and the difference: the polar rectangle has two straight radial sides, but its constant-r sides are curved arcs.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A polar rectangle is rectangular in the variables r and theta, even though it appears as a curved annular sector in the xy-plane.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the textbook-style polar diagram in a 2D SVG view. Place the origin at lower left with a black horizontal polar axis extending to the right. Draw two dashed red rays from the origin at theta = pi/6 and theta = pi/4. Draw two thick solid blue circular arcs centered at the origin with radii r = 1.5 and r = 2, only over the angular interval between the rays. Fill the annular-sector region between them with pale blue and label it R in italic serif type. Put the r labels near the corresponding blue arcs and the theta labels near the dashed rays. The Cartesian overlay should be visually secondary, such as a thin gray or orange translucent straight-sided rectangle near the same lower-left corner of R, so it compares shape without obscuring the polar region.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Sliders for r1 and r2 (pre-filled 1.5 and 2): stretch or shrink the two bounding arcs and watch the curved quadrilateral R resize between them while the angular bounds stay fixed
- Sliders for θ1 and θ2 (pre-filled π/6 and π/4): rotate the two bounding rays and watch R sweep through the new angular extent while the radial bounds stay fixed
- Toggle to overlay a straight-sided Cartesian rectangle of the same Δr × Δθ dimensions at the same corner — shows why R is only an "analogue" of a rectangle: two of its sides are curved because r is held constant on a circular arc rather than a straight line
